young.html: How do you decide what is the right thing to do? John Stuart Mill gave one famous answer: do what brings the most happiness to everyone it touches, and count everyone's happiness the same, including your own.

Mill added something important. Some kinds of happiness are higher than others. The joy of reading a great story, learning something hard, or helping a friend is worth more, he said, than the quick fun of a candy bar, even if the candy feels good too.

young.cap: Move the sliders: how many people does each choice affect, and how much? Try the late-music example.

young.html: Happiness count. Your family is choosing a Saturday activity. List three ideas. For each, guess how happy it would make each person, from 0 to 5, and add up the totals. Does the biggest total feel like the fairest choice? What if one person would be miserable?

full.html: Mill (1806–1873) was raised on the ideas of Jeremy Bentham, a friend of his father, who taught that right and wrong should be measured by pleasure and pain. Mill spent his life defending and reshaping that idea. Utilitarianism first appeared as three articles in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and as a book in 1863. Considerations on Representative Government came out in 1861. Both are in the Britannica set with On Liberty.

full.text: The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. By happiness is intended pleasure, and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain, and the privation of pleasure.
full.author: Mill

full.html: Two things make this an ethics, not selfishness. The happiness that counts is that of everyone affected; and each person counts equally. Mill quotes Bentham's rule: everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one.

full.name: gb-mill-happy
full.cap: A simple sum: people times happiness each. Try the late-music example to see the classic objection.

full.title: A simple sum
full.q: Choice A makes 12 people each 2 units happier. Choice B spares 1 person a loss of 9 units. Which has the greater total?
steps: A simple sum prefers A, 24 to 9.
full.a: A, by a simple sum. Many readers feel uneasy at this, which is why Mill's chapter on justice matters.

full.html: Critics said a life aimed at pleasure was "a doctrine worthy only of swine." Mill answered that pleasures differ in quality, not only amount. Who can judge? Those who have known both kinds.

full.text: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question.
full.author: Mill

full.html: The strongest objection is that a large total could seem to justify a serious wrong to a few. Mill's last chapter answers that the rules of justice, which protect each person's security and rights, guard the most vital part of everyone's well-being, so a society that breaks them for a short-term gain loses far more in the long run. Critics such as W. D. Ross and, later, John Rawls replied that this still makes rights depend on a sum, and that some things are wrong whatever the sum. Defenders have answered with refined versions of the theory. It remains one of the main schools of ethics.

In Considerations on Representative Government Mill argues that the best government is one in which the whole people share in ruling, through representatives they elect, because it protects everyone's interests and because taking part in public life makes citizens wiser and more active. He feared that a majority could ignore minorities, so he backed proportional representation, following Thomas Hare's plan. He argued for votes for women, and in Parliament in 1867 he proposed changing "man" to "person" in the Reform Bill; it was defeated. He also proposed extra votes for the more educated, an idea most readers then and since have rejected.
Thinking utilitarianism means "do what makes you happy." Mill insists that the agent must be as impartial as "a disinterested and benevolent spectator."

deep.text: Mill and the conversation about ethics

items: Aristotle's Ethics also puts happiness at the center, but means a life of virtue and excellence, not a sum of pleasures. Mill's higher pleasures move toward Aristotle.
Kant argued that the morality of an act lies in its motive and its rule, not its results. Mill thought Kant's test, when applied, quietly appeals to consequences.
Hume and Smith, earlier on this ladder, grounded morals in feeling and sympathy; Mill's "social feelings" build on them.
Nietzsche, later on this ladder, mocked the English moralists who made happiness the goal.
Can happiness be measured or added up?
Is it ever right to make one person suffer so that many can be happy?
Are some pleasures really better than others? Who gets to say?
Why might taking part in government make people better citizens?

questions: What is the difference between something that makes you happy for a minute and something that makes you happy for a long time?
Is the choice that makes the most people happy always the fair one?
Would you rather be "Socrates dissatisfied" or "a fool satisfied"? Why?
When your family decides something together, does everyone count the same?
Why do you think Mill wanted women to be able to vote, long before they could?
